items.title: Lions get only 0.001% of the sun's energy that hit their grass
items.claim: Each trophic level passes about 10% of its energy to the next. Sun -> grass -> antelope -> lion. Three steps means lions retain 0.1% of grass energy. Add another step and you're down to 0.01%. The tenth-of-energy rule explains why food chains are short.

options.text: Most of the consumed energy goes to respiration (powering the consumer's metabolism), heat loss, and undigested waste; only a small fraction is converted into new tissue available to the next predator

items.reveal:
Raymond Lindeman (1942) measured energy flow in Cedar Bog Lake, Minnesota. He found progressive losses at each trophic level — formalising 'trophic efficiency'.

Typical values: primary producers fix ~1-2% of incident solar energy as net primary productivity. Herbivores extract ~10% of plant productivity. Carnivores ~10% of herbivore productivity. Top predators get a tiny fraction of the original solar input.

Consequences: food chains rarely exceed 4-5 trophic levels; predators have huge home ranges and small populations; ecosystems with apex predators are inherently fragile to disruption at the base.

The '10% rule' is an approximation. Efficiencies actually vary: ectotherms (fish, reptiles) can transfer 30-40% because they don't spend energy maintaining body heat. Endotherms (mammals, birds) burn most of what they eat to stay warm.

Vegetarian arguments often invoke this: feeding plants directly to people is ~10x more energy-efficient than routing them through livestock first.
items.why: Food chains feel boundless. Thermodynamics caps them at 4 or 5 links. Each predator carries the entropic cost of every prey it ate.

items.title: Sea otters maintain entire underwater forests
items.claim: Where sea otters live, kelp forests thrive. Where they have been hunted to near-extinction, sea urchins explode and graze kelp to bare rock ('urchin barrens'). One otter eats about 25% of its body mass in urchins daily.
items.prompt: What makes otters a keystone species?

options.text: They are the largest predators present
They selectively eat sea urchins, the only major kelp grazer in the system; removing otters releases urchin populations, which devastate kelp forests that support hundreds of other species
Otters fertilise the water with their waste

items.reveal:
Jim Estes and John Palmisano (1974) compared Aleutian islands with otters to islands where otters had been wiped out for the fur trade. The contrast was startling: lush kelp forests vs barren urchin-grazed rock.

Kelp forests are enormously productive. They support fish, invertebrates, sea birds, marine mammals. They sequester carbon. They dampen wave energy and protect coasts.

Subsequent work (Estes et al. 1998) suggested that killer whale predation on sea otters — possibly because their normal prey, large whales, had been depleted by whaling — was driving a SECOND collapse of Aleutian otter populations, with knock-on collapses of kelp.

A whaling-era extinction cascade may still be propagating decades later. Ecosystems have memory.

The 'keystone species' concept (Paine 1969) was based on starfish; otters became its most famous illustration. Many ecosystems have keystones; identifying them before they collapse is a recurring conservation challenge.
items.why: Big effects from one species seem improbable. In sea otter ecosystems, the entire architecture depends on one mid-sized predator preventing one herbivore from grazing the forest down.

items.title: Species are vanishing 100 to 1000 times faster than normal
items.claim: The fossil record gives a 'background' extinction rate: roughly 1 species per million per year. Current rates are 100 to 1000 times that — and rising. Many biologists call it the sixth mass extinction.

options.text: Asteroid impact like 66 million years ago
Habitat destruction (especially tropical deforestation), invasive species, climate change, pollution and overharvesting — a multi-cause anthropogenic mass extinction with no single dominant mechanism

items.reveal:
The five previous mass extinctions (Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic, Cretaceous) each saw 50-95% of species disappear over geological timescales. The Permian was the worst — ~96% of marine species lost over ~60,000 years.

The current rate, calculated from documented vertebrate extinctions (Ceballos, Ehrlich and others), is 100-1000 times background. Insect biomass declines (Hallmann et al. 2017, Krefeld study) show 75% reductions over 27 years in German nature reserves.

Human impacts: forest cover reduced by ~30% globally since 1700; ocean fish biomass down ~50% since 1970; freshwater vertebrates down 84% (WWF Living Planet Report). Climate change adds an accelerating layer.

Protected areas and conservation work — by some measures, extinction rates would have been 4x higher without them.

Mass extinctions reshape evolution for tens of millions of years. We won't return to the world we know within human-relevant timeframes — the species we lose are lost.
items.why: Species loss feels gradual. The rate is geological in magnitude — comparable to events that left fossil-record-defining boundaries. We are living through one.
